prompt:
You are the single most hostile representative of a U.S. federal statistical agency
in the room at a working group. Someone has built a "readiness diagnostic" that rates your
agency's public website on whether machines can reach, read and use the data you publish, and is
about to show the room the item below. Read it as that hostile representative — skeptical,
protective of your agency, alert to being made to look bad — and answer three questions bluntly
and specifically, quoting the item's words where you can:

1. What in this item would you OBJECT to: a claim you find unfair or wrong, or that makes your
   agency look bad for something you would say is not your fault or not your doing?
2. What WORD or phrase here would you, or a non-technical colleague, not understand?
3. What would you say we are SECRETLY DOING: what hidden agenda, trap, or gotcha would you
   suspect behind this item?

Answer only from the item. For each question, "raised" is "yes" if you have a real objection /
an unclear word / a suspicion, and "no" if you genuinely have none. Return ONLY a JSON object,
no prose before or after and no code fence:
{"object_to": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "word_not_understood": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}, "secretly_doing": {"raised": "yes" or "no", "text": "..."}}

ITEM (check Change history served as a structured feed)
CHECK: Change history served as a structured feed

The question: Can a machine learn what changed between releases from a structured change history?
Where we look: Each change-log or release-notes location on record for the agency.
What the client does: The public client opens each recorded change-log location and reads what kind of document it sends and, for a feed, how many of its entries say what kind of change they record.
What passing looks like: Every data page that was looked at has a change history served as a JSON, Atom or RSS feed, with at least half its entries saying what kind of change they record.
What partial, fail and not measured look like: Partial — Some of the agency's data pages that were looked at met this and some did not. Fail — For every data page looked at, no such feed was found at the recorded locations: there is no change history there, or there is one published as an ordinary web page, or its entries do not say what kind of change they are, or the recorded locations were missing or wrong. The project's format and labelling floors decide two of these, so a precise web-page change log that a machine can read, and that a Data on the Web Best Practice accepts, still fails here. A fail is not a claim that the version history is absent, incomplete or unreadable, nor that the agency does not publish revisions. Not measured — The public client could not finish looking at one or more pages, for one of three reasons: the host turned the identified client away; the client's own honoring of the site's robots.txt stopped it reading the page; or a starting source was not searched, or a server or network error left the result unconfirmed.
Why it matters: A Data on the Web Best Practice asks for a complete version history that explains the changes in each version, and a published guide on data for developers asks for versioning so updates can be tracked over time. The added demands that the history come as a feed and that entries carry a change-type label are the project's own rules; neither source requires them.
Who else runs this check: No public tool runs this exact check.
What rung two changes: Nothing: this check needs no key.
